Visible injuries or wounds on others

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same node's strong intrusive, poorly controlled re-experiencing items ('triggered without warning' and 'full sensory reliving'). Severe reliving can coexist with disclosure, but 'very easily' pulls in the opposite direction and is the clearest within-node inconsistency.

issues.item: Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: The cognitive formulation leaves Threat disconnected from the active network, yet 'Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time' implies a strong ongoing sense of current threat. That threat-focused appraisal is not supported by the formulation and is not matched by any Threat-node content.

issues.item: Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
issues.explanation: 'Entrapment: Having no options' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The negative appraisals and memory content center on global damage/self-reliance and sensory reliving, not on themes of being trapped or unable to escape, so this trigger appears insufficiently grounded in the reported formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Physical Stress' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The triggers and appraisals do not indicate body-strain or exertion as a salient trauma-linked theme, making this strategy look disconnected from the reported trigger-memory-appraisal pattern.

The trigger profile is centered on entrapment, touch, and a specific taste, which implies reactivity to concrete sensory or situational reminders of the witnessed trauma. 'Entrapment: Having no options' is harder to reconcile with the rest of the profile because the memory and appraisal items do not describe being trapped or immobilized; they emphasize sensory reliving, nonverbal memory, hypervigilance, and global damage/self-doubt rather than a trapped-state theme. For a witnessed-trauma case, this item stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Physical Stress' is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The selected triggers and memory items point to sensory cue-driven reliving, and the appraisals concern vigilance, self-reliance, and life damage. Avoiding bodily stress suggests fear of physiological arousal or somatic activation, but there are no corresponding threat or appraisal items about bodily danger, losing control when activated, or physical collapse. It therefore looks like a maladaptive strategy targeting a symptom pattern not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Reminders' appears mis-keyed: the strategy should be an avoidant behavior (e.g., avoiding being reminded), but the selected text describes a trigger/reminder rather than something the patient does. This makes the maladaptive-strategy item internally incoherent.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: The profile includes a prominent current-threat appraisal ('I have to be on guard all the time') despite Threat being structurally inactive: there are no active edges to or from Threat, and the rest of the profile is dominated by memory-based reexperiencing, negative self-appraisals, and coping strategies rather than an active external-danger formulation. This item fits Threat more than Negative Appraisals and is inconsistent with the specified formulation.

vignette: David is thirty years old, a carpenter who spends his days cutting and shaping hardwood in a bustling workshop in suburban Illinois. One autumn afternoon, while sawing a piece of pine for a client, he watched the apprentice’s hand slip on a splinter and the apprentice fall onto the floor, a sharp crack in the wood mirroring the sudden, raw scream that cut through the shop. The apprentice’s arm shattered, and the blood pooled like spilled paint across the floorboards. The scene was brief, yet the image of the fractured limb, the taste of metal on the apprentice’s lips, and the feel of the apprentice’s trembling palm pressed against the saw's handle left a lasting imprint. David was not injured, but he felt a surge of terror that clung to his chest, and from that day forward the workshop became a living tableau of his trauma. The next morning, as he reached for a hammer, the echo of that hammer’s click reverberated in his mind, reminding him of the apprentice’s frantic grip. The tactile memory of the tool’s vibration triggered a full sensory reliving: the bright glare of the workshop lights, the sharp scent of sawdust, and even the faint metallic taste he could almost taste when he closed his mouth. In the midst of this, his fingers tightened on the hammer, and he unconsciously shoved his hand to a nearby bucket of canned beans, eating a large handful to numb the ache that rattled his chest. The taste of the beans—flat and unremarkable—did not soothe him; instead, it reminded him of the apprentice’s broken bite, a gustatory echo that made his mouth ache. He also found himself deliberately stepping away from the workbench, the urge to escape so intense that he could not even bring himself to think about what had happened. Each of these actions—overeating, dissociating, avoiding thoughts—became his way to keep the scene from tearing through him. He began to believe that if he could avoid the workshop’s noises, the sight of any injured hand, or even a fleeting memory of a sharp taste, he could protect himself. That belief deepened his sense that his life was irrevocably shattered and that he could no longer trust his own judgment. When the memory resurfaced without warning—often in the middle of a conversation or when a hammer clanged in the background—David’s mind could not translate the terror into words. He felt the full weight of the injury, the sound of blood, the apprentice’s cry. The intensity of these memories reinforced his negative appraisal that his life was destroyed, that he was permanently damaged, and that he could not rely on his own resilience. He began to perceive every tool, every glint of metal, and even the taste of a sour candy as a potential reminder of that day, turning the very environment that sustained his work into a constant reminder of his broken self. The realization that each of these triggers could reignite the vivid, all-sensory reliving of the event made him even more vigilant, making him more susceptible to the same sensory cues that would, in turn, spark the memories again. His avoidance of thoughts and his deliberate dissociation, which he used to escape the terror, only deepened the conviction that he could not rely on himself to manage the trauma. As the cycle tightened, the shame and frustration he felt when he overate or fled the workshop grew, reinforcing the notion that his life had been permanently altered and that he could no longer face normal work or conversation without fearing a return of the nightmare. Now, months later, David’s hands tremble as he grips a chisel, and he frequently takes a break to empty his stomach of quick, sugary snacks, hoping the taste will dull the ache in his chest. His avoidance has begun to affect his relationship with his wife, who worries that he is withdrawing from family meals and social gatherings, fearing that the scent of food might spark another flashback. The weight of his own perception that his life has been destroyed sits heavy on his shoulders. The reason he finally sought help is that the relentless cycle of triggers, memories, and negative beliefs has begun to sap his ability to perform his craft, and he fears that if he cannot break this loop, he will lose not only his job but also his sense of identity. He wishes to reclaim the feeling that he can rely on himself, to feel safe enough to work, and to find a way to speak about the day he witnessed the apprentice’s injury, even if only in fragments, and not just in the vivid, all-sensory flashes that continue to haunt him.
